name: LuaJIT Remake (Deegen)
workload: Lua benchmark set in luabench/ (includes fasta, k-nucleotide and revcomp programs), 5 repeats each, geometric mean over all benchmarks, run pinned to one core with taskset.
claimed_speedup: Interpreter is 34.6% faster than LuaJIT's interpreter and 185% faster than the official PUC Lua 5.1 interpreter (geometric mean over benchmarks).
compiler_and_flags: Release build via python3 ljr-build make release (docker image, CC=clang CXX=clang++, cmake BUILD_FLAVOR=RELEASE, Ninja); exact optimisation flags not stated in README. Baselines run with GC turned off to match.
hardware: Intel i7-12700H laptop, 32GB DDR4 (stated in README footnote)
tradeoffs: x86-64 Linux only; build needs docker; interpreter and runtime are generated automatically from a semantic description of the bytecodes (Deegen), so the design is reusable for other languages. Table implementation uses hidden classes rather than a plain hash table.
caveats: Claim is for the interpreter tier only, versus LuaJIT's interpreter, not LuaJIT's trace JIT, which is much faster on hot loops. The README says the JIT tiers are still in progress (a search snippet of the author's blog says the baseline JIT beat LuaJIT on 13 of 44 benchmarks but was about 34% slower on geometric average; snippet only, the blog was blocked). GC is not implemented, so the baselines were run with GC off; the package library (require/module) and some stdlib are missing; Lua 5.1 only. Optimisation flags are not in the README, so tier C rather than A; the benchmark programs and run_bench.sh are public.
found_via: WebSearch: 'JIT compiler C++ benchmark faster than LuaJIT github' led to the repo, then opened its README, run_bench.sh and ljr-build.

name: libriscv
baseline: LuaJIT (JIT mode); README also compares against wasmtime, wasm3 and Luau
workload: Embedded scripting micro-benchmarks run in the sandbox as RISC-V guest code with binary translation, versus the same tasks as LuaJIT scripts: host-to-guest call overhead, syscall cost, integer math loops, sieve of 10M.
claimed_speedup: Binary-translated libriscv vs LuaJIT gist (median): call overhead 2 ns vs 156 ns, syscall (0 args) 10 ns vs 174 ns, integer math 6 ns vs 52 ns, sieve(10M) 80 ms vs 123 ms; fib(40) row shows parity (66 ns median both).
hardware: Gist does not state the CPU; the README names a Ryzen 7950X for its other charts (CoreMark 38223 vs 41382 native, about 92%).
stars_or_usage: 1.1k stars; same organisation maintains godot-sandbox (487 stars)
tradeoffs: Emulator and sandbox for precompiled RISC-V programs rather than a general JIT for a dynamic language; full binary translation needs a C compiler (GCC or TCC) at run time, or the generated C99 can be embedded ahead of time for platforms that forbid executable memory. Needs a RISC-V toolchain to build guest code.
caveats: Comparison is not like for like: guest code is C/C++ compiled to RISC-V, LuaJIT runs Lua scripts. The numbers come from author-run gists with no CPU or flags on the gist page, and the workloads are hand-picked for game scripting. README claims such as 'routinely faster than other interpreters, JIT-compilers and binary translators', '3 ns call latency' and 'can call the above function 5.25-7.25 times before wasmtime has called it once' are first-party; the fib(40) row is a tie.
found_via: GitHub topics page github.com/topics/jit?l=c%2B%2B (ranked 7th by stars), then the README and the LuaJIT comparison gist.

name: TPDE
workload: TPDE-LLVM back-end compiling LLVM IR to x86-64 and AArch64 machine code, intended as a baseline compiler for JIT use or unoptimised builds.
claimed_speedup: TPDE-LLVM compiles 10--20x faster than LLVM -O0 with similar code quality (README sentence).
stars_or_usage: 671 stars; integrates with Clang/Flang via patch
tradeoffs: Only ELF x86-64 and AArch64 targets; code quality is -O0 level by design; the LLVM back-end is usable as library (JIT), standalone tool tpde-llc or Clang patch (LLVM 19 to 21 patches). Framework also supports other SSA IRs.
caveats: README gives only the one-line ratio. The paper (Schwarz, Kamm, Engelke, arXiv 2505.22610, camera-ready at CGO 2026) was blocked here; a search snippet of its abstract says 8-26x faster than LLVM -O0 and 8-24x on SPECint 2017 with run-time performance within +-9%, so a reader with paper access can raise this to tier B or A (artifact record on zenodo). Compares compile time against LLVM's -O0 pipeline, which is not itself one of the listed JIT baselines.
found_via: WebSearch: 'copy-and-patch JIT github C++ benchmark faster than LLVM baseline compiler' surfaced the paper; WebSearch for TPDE details, then opened the github.com repo page and README.

name: Codon
baseline: PyPy 3 (also CPython 3 and Node/V8 and LuaJIT in the same shootout)
workload: Single-threaded benchmarks-game programs (binarytrees, brainfuck, fasta, k-nucleotide, matmul, nbody, spectralnorm, mandelbrot, fannkuchredux) written in simple Python, best of several runs, from kostya's jit-benchmarks round 1 (2023-02-28).
claimed_speedup: Best time in seconds, Codon vs PyPy3 (shootout table): binarytrees 1.0 vs 3.84, brainfuck 2.05 vs 8.77, brainfuck2 1.91 vs 11.03, fasta 1.66 vs 3.19, knucleotide 2.69 vs 3.7, matmul 0.25 vs 0.36, nbody 2.23 vs 4.44, spectralnorm 0.53 vs 0.71; PyPy3 wins mandelbrot 0.54 vs 0.65 and fannkuchredux 0.71 vs 1.82. Codon README separately: fib(40) 17.98 s CPython vs 0.28 s Codon and 'typical speedups over vanilla Python are on the order of 10-100x'.
compiler_and_flags: Docker-based harness in the shootout repo; compiler versions and flags are not on the README page.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 3800X, 80GB DDR4-3200, docker on Ubuntu 22.10 (shootout README)
tradeoffs: Ahead-of-time compiler for a statically typed Python dialect, not a drop-in Python implementation: no full dynamic semantics and limited CPython library coverage, with a Python interop bridge. It also has a JIT mode (the repo has a jit directory) and multithreading and GPU extensions that PyPy lacks.
caveats: Independent third-party shootout from 2023 with an older Codon release; Codon produced no result for pidigits, regexdna and revcomp, and Node (V8) and LuaJIT beat Codon on several rows (fannkuchredux, mandelbrot, nbody, spectralnorm). It is an AOT compiler rather than a tracing JIT, so it fits this category loosely. The exaloop.io benchmark page was not reachable. The repo's own bench/ directory only runs Codon and does not include PyPy, so the PyPy evidence is the third-party table. Single benchmark author, and the shootout page does not list compiler flags (tier B, not A).
found_via: WebSearch: 'Python JIT compiler written in C++ faster than PyPy benchmark github' surfaced kostya/jit-benchmarks; Codon rows extracted from its README table.

name: FakeLua
workload: 51 Lua micro-scenarios in 6 categories (algorithms, strings, tables, function calls, ...), Google Benchmark harness bench_mark, FakeLua JIT_GCC and JIT_TCC backends versus Lua 5.4 and hand-written C++.
claimed_speedup: JIT_GCC vs Lua 5.4: Fibonacci n=32 36.6x (297.9 ms vs 6.8 ms), Sum n=5M 30.4x, Popcount n=100K 37.3x, FloatPoly n=1M 34.9x, TailRecursion 107.5x; TCC backend Fibonacci 11.2x. Many table and string rows are only 1.0-4.8x and regex rows are slower (0.06-0.21x).
compiler_and_flags: Release build, -O3 -DNDEBUG; GCC 15.1.0 for the JIT_GCC run (GCC 16.2.0 for the interpreter run); Lua 5.4.7
hardware: AMD EPYC 7K62 48-core (GCC JIT run, 2026-08-14); AMD EPYC 7551 (interpreter run, 2026-09-16)
tradeoffs: Runs a Lua 5.4 subset: no coroutines, metatables or require, and no implicit string-number coercion; arena allocation with per-frame reset instead of GC. JIT_GCC shells out to the system GCC at run time (compile latency and a compiler dependency); JIT_TCC uses embedded TinyCC; JIT_INTERP bytecode VM needs no compiler.
caveats: Baseline is PUC Lua, not LuaJIT, so the result does not show a win over LuaJIT. Compile time is not in the timed region (scripts are compiled at init). The project's own harness; the bytecode interpreter tier is 1.3x to 7.6x slower than Lua 5.4 in its own algorithm rows, and the hand-written C++ references in some rows are folded by the compiler. Very young repository.
found_via: GitHub topics page github.com/topics/jit?l=c%2B%2B&o=desc&s=stars (item 19), then README and benchmark/README.md.

name: Eclipse OpenJ9
workload: DayTrader7 on WebSphere Liberty with DB2 on a second machine: startup time to 'ready to run a smarter planet', RSS footprint after startup and during load, ramp-up and peak throughput.
claimed_speedup: 51 - 55% faster startup, 45 - 57% smaller startup footprint, 33% smaller footprint during application ramp-up, comparable throughput (OpenJ9 with shared class cache and dynamic AOT versus HotSpot).
compiler_and_flags: OpenJDK 11.0.8 with OpenJ9 (build master-78f76052e) vs OpenJDK 11.0.7 HotSpot, both AdoptOpenJDK binaries; OpenJ9 configs: defaults, SCC plus AOT, SCC plus AOT with -Xtune:virtualized; heap -Xmx256m or -Xms256m -Xmx256m for startup, 1G for load.
hardware: Desktop 4-core Intel i7-3770K @ 3.50GHz, 16GB RAM, CentOS 7.7; Java process pinned to 2 cores; JMeter on a third machine
tradeoffs: The win is startup time and memory footprint, not peak throughput. Needs a shared class cache populated by a prior cold run for the startup gain; the AOT code is slightly larger than JIT code. Builds are AdoptOpenJDK-style OpenJDK binaries with the OpenJ9 VM and JIT in place of HotSpot.
caveats: First-party IBM-run results from 2020 (JDK 11); without the SCC the page says OpenJ9 and HotSpot start at similar speed. Benchmark application depends on WebSphere Liberty and DB2, so it is not easy to reproduce, and the harness is not published (tier C). Newer JDK 17 results on eclipse.dev (blocked here; search snippet only) were quoted as 10-30% faster DayTrader8 startup and 31-38% smaller footprint. Repo README itself gives no numbers.
found_via: Assigned category check of JVM JITs: opened openj9 repo page (no numbers), then WebSearch 'Eclipse OpenJ9 vs HotSpot startup time footprint benchmark', then openj9-website repo benchmark/openjdk11-daytrader7.md via raw.githubusercontent.com.

name: WAVM
baseline: V8 WebAssembly (Chromium 78 via Webassembly.sh), also Firefox 70, wasmtime 0.8.0, Wasmer 0.13.1
workload: CoreMark 1.0 compiled to WebAssembly and run in each engine.
claimed_speedup: CoreMark score 14946.57 for WAVM vs 6914.33 Chromium 78, 7251.15 Firefox 70, 6453.51 wasmtime 0.8.0 (--optimize), 12450.20 Wasmer 0.13.1 LLVM, 1627.87 wasm3; about 2.2x Chromium (derived from page data); native GCC 7.4.0 64-bit 19144.86.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the wasm build; native build GCC 7.4.0. The wasm3 doc links its wasm-coremark repo for how to run it.
tradeoffs: Compiles WebAssembly to machine code with LLVM (build depends on LLVM); uses virtual memory and signal handlers for bounds-checked memory accesses; intended for non-browser applications.
caveats: Numbers come from a competitor's document (wasm3) measured in 2019-2020 on old engine versions (Chromium 78, wasmtime 0.8.0, Wasmer 0.13.1), and the page itself says they are kept as a historical record, not a current comparison. WAVM's own README makes only qualitative claims ('close to native', 'can even beat native in some cases') with no numbers. Compile and start-up time are not part of the score. Ranked as independent measurement of a well-known suite (CoreMark) but it falls short of A.
found_via: Browsing wasm-runtime lists; opened WAVM repo page (no numbers) and found its row in wasm3 docs/Performance.md.

name: WebAssembly Micro Runtime (WAMR)
workload: WAMR AOT-compiled modules (wamrc) and WAMR interpreters versus wasm3 on CoreMark, a matrix multiply and gimli on x86-64, and matrix, gimli and seqhash on a Cortex-M7 board.
claimed_speedup: wamr-aot / wasm3 on x86-64: matrix 22.02x, gimli 9.94x, CoreMark 8.79x; on Cortex-M7: matrix 30.17x, gimli 19.13x, seqhash 21.12x; wamr-aot reaches 0.79x of native GCC -O3 on CoreMark. wasm3 itself is 1.07-1.32x faster than WAMR's interpreters on x86-64.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 7.5.0 -O3 (x86-64), arm-zephyr-eabi-gcc 9.2.0 -Os (Cortex-M7); wasm3 version not stated
hardware: Intel Core i7-7700 @ 3.60GHz, Ubuntu 18.04 (x86-64); Nucleo F767ZI Cortex-M7 board on Zephyr
tradeoffs: Also offers Fast JIT and LLVM JIT tiers, a fast interpreter (about 2x the classic interpreter) and a small classic interpreter; ~29.4K aot runtime and ~56-59K interpreter text size on Cortex-M4f per README. AOT needs a separate wamrc compile step.
caveats: The wiki numbers are from 2020-09-01 and compare WAMR's AOT mode with an interpreter (wasm3), so the baseline is not a JIT and is not one of the listed incumbents; the wiki shows WAMR's own interpreters slower than wasm3. No comparison to V8 or another JIT on that page, though the README lists JetStream2, PolyBench, CoreMark and Sightglass sections. Wiki run is first-party.
found_via: GitHub topics page github.com/topics/jit?l=c&o=desc&s=stars (WAMR first), then README and the wiki Performance page.

name: Pyston
workload: Web-serving macrobenchmarks (README does not name them or give a table).
claimed_speedup: Pyston 'full' (CPython 3.8.12 fork with DynASM JIT, quickening and attribute caching) is roughly 30% faster than CPython on web serving macrobenchmarks; Pyston 'lite' (JIT extension module for Python 3.7 to 3.10) roughly 10% faster.
tradeoffs: Fork is API compatible but not ABI compatible with CPython, so C extensions must be rebuilt; pinned to Python 3.8 (full) or 3.7 to 3.10 (lite); lite installs with pip. Technique list: low-overhead JIT using DynASM, quickening, aggressive attribute caching.
caveats: Repository description says no longer maintained. README gives rounded percentages with no hardware, harness or per-benchmark data (details were on the Pyston blog, which was not opened). Does not compare against PyPy, whose JIT is much faster on many benchmarks. Implemented in C as a CPython fork, so it is usable from C/C++ only via the Python embedding API.
found_via: Assigned-category check of Python JITs: opened github.com/pyston/pyston and its README on raw.githubusercontent.com.

name: RVVM
workload: RISC-V guest emulation with a tracing JIT (RVJIT) with x86_64, ARM64 and RISC-V host backends; no workload named.
claimed_speedup: README bullet: 'Tracing JIT with x86_64, ARM64, RISC-V backends - Faster than QEMU TCG'. No numbers given.
tradeoffs: Library under MPL-2.0 and binaries under GPL-3.0; JNI bindings are MPL-2.0. Runs Linux, Haiku, FreeBSD and OpenBSD guests; also userland emulation.
caveats: Tier D: bare claim, no benchmark, hardware or QEMU version. QEMU is not one of the listed incumbents. Included as the single notable tier D record of this run.
found_via: GitHub topics page github.com/topics/jit?l=c&o=desc&s=stars (4th), then README.
